summary: SmartFarm AI helps a farmer choose a crop for the next season using only NASA data. The farmer marks the four corners of a field on a satellite map. The app then automatically retrieves NASA observations for that exact location: 10 years of temperature and rainfall (NASA POWER), frost and heat days, satellite rainfall (GPM IMERG), and the latest soil moisture and soil texture (SMAP Level 4). It screens five crops (wheat, barley, maize, sunflower, chickpeas) against temperature, water need and soil, finds the best growing months for each crop, and shows the irrigation needed in mm and m³. The farmer sees one suggested crop, six key facts and the main risks, with a link to the NASA source for every number. Everything is automatic and works from 85°S to 85°N, so farms without sensors or soil tests can still use NASA data. If data is missing, the app says so instead of guessing. It is a preliminary screen to support local advice, not a yield prediction.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

A farmer searches for a place (or uses their location) and clicks four corners around a field on a satellite map. The app calculates the area and, about 0.7 seconds after the last corner, automatically fetches NASA data for the field centre. It then shows a suggested crop, the growing months, average temperature, rainfall, extra water needed (mm and m³ for the whole field), soil type, current soil moisture and the main risks. Full observations, source links and limitations open on request and can be downloaded as JSON.

HOW IT WORKS

- NASA POWER (MERRA-2) monthly: 10 years of temperature and rainfall.

- NASA POWER daily: frost days (<0°C), heat days (>=35°C) and root-zone wetness for the last full year.

- GPM IMERG (via POWER): satellite rainfall for the last full year, used as a second rainfall check.

- SMAP Level 4 (SPL4SMGP v008): latest surface and root-zone soil moisture, 9 km grid.

- SMAP Level 4 land-model constants (SPL4SMLM v008): clay and sand fractions, used to estimate soil texture without a soil test.

For each crop the app searches the field's own 10-year climate for the months whose temperature fits the crop and that have the most rain. It counts 80% of seasonal rainfall as usable, shows the irrigation needed to reach the crop's lower water need, and blocks crops for temperature, poor drainage or measured salinity. Water needs and salt tolerance come from FAO references.

BENEFITS

Free (open NASA data), no sensors, works anywhere from 85°S to 85°N, fully automatic (only four corners needed), plain language, and every number links to its NASA source and date. Anything the farmer knows (soil, water supply, season, local crops) overrides the automatic estimate.

INTENDED IMPACT

Better-informed crop choices before money is spent on seed, a shared evidence starting point for agricultural advisers, and crops matched to the water that is really available.

TOOLS

TypeScript, React, Vite, Leaflet, Node.js. NASA POWER API, NASA CMR and OPeNDAP for SMAP. Esri imagery, OpenStreetMap. Git and automated tests (24 passing). Tested live at 7 land locations on six continents.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

1) Soil type without a soil test: we reuse the clay and sand values inside NASA's SMAP model. 2) The growing season is found from each field's own climate, not assumed, and works in both hemispheres. 3) The app says "I don't know": if essential data is missing, no crop is suggested and no values are invented.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Satellite data is regional (9-50 km), so results are labelled as estimates. Farmer knowledge overrides NASA estimates. Simplicity for non-experts. Privacy: nothing is stored and NASA receives only the field-centre coordinates. Security: the NASA access token stays on the server. Honest limits: five crops, general FAO-based thresholds that are not tuned per region, no yield prediction, not yet validated against real harvests.
